title: Our Lady of Fatima (13 May)
hookLine: three shepherd children in Portugal in 1917, asking for prayer and penance

cards: May 1917. Europe is at war, and Portugal has sent its own soldiers to the trenches.
In the hills near a village called Fatima, three children are watching sheep: Lucia, ten, and her younger cousins Francisco and Jacinta, eight and seven.
Around noon on the thirteenth, they later said, a flash like lightning came, and then a lady brighter than the sun, standing over a small oak tree.
She asked them to come back on the thirteenth of every month, and to pray the rosary every day, for peace in the world and the end of the war.

teach.b: The children kept coming back, month after month through October. In August the local administrator held them, and that meeting came days late, away from the usual spot.

The crowds grew from a handful of neighbors to thousands. On the thirteenth of October, in pouring rain, a huge crowd gathered, and witnesses, a reporter among them, described the sun seeming to spin and plunge.
People still argue over what they saw.

teach.h: PRAY, DO PENANCE, PRAY FOR PEACE.
teach.b: The message the children carried was simple and demanding: pray, especially the rosary; do penance; make sacrifices for sinners; pray for peace.
Francisco and Jacinta took it so seriously that they offered up small hungers and discomforts, the way children would. Both died young, in the flu epidemic that followed the war, in 1919 and 1920.

In 2017, a hundred years after the first appearance, Pope Francis canonized them at Fatima, two children named saints not for dying as martyrs but for how they lived. Lucia became a nun and lived until 2005.
The Church judged the Fatima appearances worthy of belief in 1930, and popes have gone there on pilgrimage. But Catholic teaching calls these private revelations.
They add nothing to the faith; the Church allows and encourages devotion to them, and does not require any Catholic to believe them.
What Fatima asks for, though, is old: the rosary, and Mary as the one who points to her son.

teach.h: ALL GENERATIONS SHALL CALL ME BLESSED.
teach.b: As she said in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "all generations shall call me blessed." On the thirteenth of May, some Catholics pray a decade for peace.

how: On 13 May Catholics often pray the rosary for peace, and pilgrims gather at the shrine in Fatima, Portugal, for candlelight processions; the appearances are approved as worthy of belief, but Catholics are not required to believe in them.

games.q: you're one of the children. the lady asks you to come back on the thirteenth of every month. the village is skeptical. what do you do?
o: tell no one and go once.
games.why: they kept coming back through October (in August, held by the local administrator, they came days late), and the crowds grew from a handful of neighbors to thousands.

practice: A decade of the rosary is one Our Father, ten Hail Marys and one Glory Be; if you pray, you can pray one now, on beads or on your fingers, for one place at war, naming the place first.
If you don't pray, sit with the name of that place, and the children there, for ten slow breaths, and then a few more.

wordCard.voice: Fatima. The Portuguese village where three shepherd children said Mary appeared in 1917, asking for the rosary, penance and prayers for peace. Her day is the thirteenth of May. Today's word.

orig.note: Portuguese: Our Lady of Fatima, the name of the shrine and the feast.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for peace. Ten Hail Marys, one place, one name. See you tomorrow.
